title: Two-step sign-in and a password manager: set up in ten minutes

narration: Say your colleague Sam
uses one password on an old shopping site,
and the same one at work.
beats.visual_intent: Sam at a work laptop; two sign-in screens side by side, a shopping site and the company sign-in, the same masked password typed into both.

grounding.claim: Sam reuses one password at work and on a shopping site

narration: The shopping site leaks.
Someone tries that password at work,
and Sam's account opens.
beats.visual_intent: The shopping site card cracks and the password slips out; a stranger's cursor types it into the company sign-in page, clicks Sign in, and the inbox opens.

grounding.claim: a leaked password tried on another site can open it
reuse lets one leak open a work account

narration: Two settings, a few minutes,
and a leaked password stops being enough.
beats.visual_intent: The two settings appear as two toggles on a clean settings screen, both switching on.

grounding.claim: with two-step sign-in a leaked password alone is not enough

narration: A password alone fails three ways.
Reuse: one leak opens every account.
Phishing: a fake page collects it.
Leaked lists: old passwords get tried everywhere.
beats.visual_intent: Three tiles light one by one as named: one key opening several doors, a look-alike sign-in page, a long scrolling list of masked passwords.

grounding.claim: reuse means one leak can open every account using that password
phishing gets people to type passwords into fake pages
breached passwords circulate in lists tried against other accounts

beats.misconception: a strong password is enough on its own

narration: Two-step sign-in adds a second proof:
something you know, your password,
plus something you have, your phone.
beats.visual_intent: The sign-in page gains a second step: the password field on the laptop, then a phone beside it showing a code.

grounding.claim: two-step sign-in is something you know plus something you have

concepts: something you know plus something you have

narration: It's not unhackable,
but a stolen password alone no longer gets in.
beats.visual_intent: A stranger's cursor types a stolen password; the page moves to the code step and waits, with no way forward.

grounding.claim: two-step sign-in is not a guarantee
a stolen password alone is no longer enough

beats.misconception: two-step sign-in makes an account unhackable

narration: On your laptop, open Security settings.
Find two-step sign-in, and click Turn on.
beats.visual_intent: Screencast: the cursor opens the account menu, clicks Security, scrolls to Two-step sign-in and clicks Turn on, each control highlighted as it is named.

grounding.claim: typical steps start in security settings with turning on two-step sign-in

narration: Choose Authenticator app,
and a QR code appears.
beats.visual_intent: Screencast: a method picker; the cursor clicks Authenticator app and a QR code fades in on the laptop screen.

grounding.claim: you choose authenticator app and a QR code is shown

narration: On your phone, open the authenticator app,
tap Add account,
and point the camera at the code.
beats.visual_intent: The phone slides in beside the laptop; a finger taps Add account, the camera view frames the QR code on the laptop screen.

grounding.claim: you scan the QR code with the authenticator app

narration: That scan shares a secret key once.
Now the app shows a six-digit code,
new about every thirty seconds.
beats.visual_intent: The account appears in the app with a six-digit code and a small countdown ring that runs out and refreshes to a new code.

grounding.claim: the app generates one-time codes from a secret key shared at the QR scan
codes are six digits
codes change about every 30 seconds

narration: Type the current code into the laptop,
and click Verify.
beats.visual_intent: Screencast: the six digits are typed into the laptop's code box, matching the phone; the cursor clicks Verify and a confirmation tick appears.

grounding.claim: you type the current code to confirm
you type the code currently on screen

narration: Next come backup codes, usually shown only once.
Each works one time, if your phone isn't there.
beats.visual_intent: Screencast: a panel of short backup codes; one code is highlighted and marked as single use.

grounding.claim: backup codes are usually shown at setup, often only once
each backup code typically works once as a stand-in

narration: Keep them off the phone you might lose:
in your password manager, or where IT says.
beats.visual_intent: The backup codes lift off the screen; a crossed-out phone on one side, a password manager vault and an IT note on the other; the codes settle into the vault.

grounding.claim: store backup codes safely and separately from the phone, e.g. in the password manager, per company policy

recall.prompt: Where do your backup codes go?

narration: The password manager is an encrypted vault,
opened with one master password.
beats.visual_intent: Screencast: the password manager's unlock screen, one password field, the vault opening onto a list of saved logins.

grounding.claim: a password manager is an encrypted vault unlocked by one master password

narration: Make it a long passphrase you'll remember.
It usually can't be recovered for you.
beats.visual_intent: A short password grows into a long phrase of several words in the unlock field; a small strength bar fills.

grounding.claim: the master password should be a long memorable passphrase
the vendor usually cannot recover a forgotten master password

narration: Sign in to a site as usual.
When the manager offers, click Save.
beats.visual_intent: Screencast: a generic site's sign-in; after sign-in a small manager prompt drops down and the cursor clicks Save; the login appears in the vault list.

grounding.claim: you save a login by accepting the manager's offer after signing in

narration: For a reused password, open Change password
and click Generate:
long, random, and unique to this account.
beats.visual_intent: Screencast: the site's Change password form; the cursor clicks the manager's Generate button and a long random password fills the field.

grounding.claim: managers generate long random unique passwords
replace weak or reused passwords with generated ones

narration: Save it, and autofill types it for you,
but only on the address it was saved for.
beats.visual_intent: Screencast: Save clicked; later the sign-in page opens and the fields fill themselves, the address bar highlighted.

grounding.claim: autofill normally fills only on the saved site address

narration: A look-alike page that won't fill in by itself
is a warning sign, not a glitch.
beats.visual_intent: Before and after: the real address fills, a look-alike address with one letter changed stays empty and is flagged.

grounding.claim: no autofill on a look-alike page is a warning sign, not a guarantee

narration: Now your phone is gone.
What would you do first?
beats.visual_intent: An empty desk spot where the phone was; the laptop shows the code step waiting.

grounding.claim: the viewer has lost their phone

beats.misconception: if I lose my phone I am locked out for good

narration: One, sign in with a backup code.
Two, tell IT straight away.
on_screen: 1 Sign in with a backup code
beats.visual_intent: A short numbered path builds: step 1 with a backup code typed into the code box, step 2 with a message to IT.

grounding.claim: sign in with a backup code and report the loss to IT promptly
reporting quickly lets IT revoke access and check the account

narration: Three, set up your new phone.
Four, remove the old device
and sign out other sessions.
on_screen: 1 Sign in with a backup code
beats.visual_intent: The same path continues: step 3 with a new phone scanning a code, step 4 with the old device crossed off a device list.

grounding.claim: set up the authenticator again, remove the old device, sign out other sessions

narration: Tempted to turn two-step sign-in off?
That drops your protection.
Move it to the new phone instead.
beats.visual_intent: The two-step toggle is pulled toward off and marked wrong; then the code moves from the old phone to the new phone, marked right.

grounding.claim: the right move is to set up the authenticator on the new phone
without the second step a password alone is enough again

narration: Back to Sam.
The same leaked password,
and this time it stops at the code screen.
beats.visual_intent: The hook's stranger cursor types Sam's leaked password into the company sign-in; the page halts on the code step, while Sam's phone holds the code.

grounding.claim: a leaked password alone no longer gets in with two-step sign-in

narration: Turn it on today,
store your backup codes,
and swap one reused password this week.
beats.visual_intent: Three checklist items tick off over the laptop and phone together.

grounding.claim: store backup codes per company policy
replace reused passwords with generated ones
